Karmayoga, "the yoga of action," takes up the question Arjuna presses at the outset: if wisdom is better than action, as chapter 2 seemed to say, why does Kṛṣṇa still urge him to fight? Kṛṣṇa answers by denying the premise — no one can remain without acting even for a moment, since everyone is driven to act by the guṇas of nature (verses 4-8) — and then reframes what action itself can be. The middle of the chapter reads the old Vedic cycle of sacrifice as a figure for unattached action: gods and men sustain one another through yajña, and the chain of dependence traced from rain to food to beings is grounded, at last, in brahman itself (verses 9-16). Kṛṣṇa then holds up the free man, exemplified by the philosopher-king Janaka and by Kṛṣṇa's own case, who acts with nothing left to gain, solely for loka-saṃgraha, "the world's welfare" — and asks Arjuna to act the same way, without unsettling those who still cling to the fruits of their own work (verses 17-29). Kṛṣṇa then turns to command Arjuna directly: surrender every action to him and fight, free of anguish (verse 30); those who follow this teaching in faith are freed from action, while those who only carp at it are lost and without understanding (verses 31-32); forcible restraint of the senses accomplishes nothing against a nature that will act as it must (verse 33), so it is passion and aversion themselves, not the senses' contact with their objects, that must be mastered as the true waylayers of the self (verse 34) — which is why one's own dharma, however imperfectly kept, is better than another's well performed (verse 35). The chapter's second half turns to the real obstacle to such freedom: not action itself but kāma, desire, which wears the mask of anger and covers wisdom the way smoke covers fire, dust a mirror, or a caul an unborn child (verses 36-39). Its remedy is a discipline of hierarchy — senses, mind, understanding, and beyond all of these the self — mastered by force of that highest self, with which the chapter closes.
